why: Holmes addresses the narrator as "Watson" in ¶3, and the narrator is the first-person teller.
¶2 places the narrator in bed, with Holmes standing by the side of it.
¶1 says the narrator has "my notes" of the seventy-odd cases.

text: That morning, before a quarter-past seven: Mrs. Hudson is knocked up
why: ¶3 says Mrs. Hudson has already been knocked up that morning, which fits happening before Holmes woke Watson at 7:15.

text: Early April, ’83, a quarter-past seven in the morning: Holmes wakes Watson
why: ¶2 gives early April, the year '83, and a quarter-past seven when Holmes is standing by the bed.

text: During the last month before Watson writes: the lady to whom the pledge was given dies
why: ¶1 says the narrator was freed from the pledge during the last month by the untimely death of the lady to whom it was given.

text: Some time before Watson writes: the death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott
why: ¶1 mentions widespread rumours about the death of Dr. Grimesby Roylott, so the death is referred to before the narrator writes.

text: When Watson writes, after the death of the lady to whom the pledge was given
why: Follows from ¶1: the narrator writes after the lady's death, which freed him from the pledge.

text: What Holmes had from Mrs. Hudson
why: The story does not say Holmes received any account from Mrs. Hudson. ¶3 only says she was knocked up and is a quip; no information from her has been given.
Holmes's visit at dawn with a "common lot" remark suggests he has something to tell. The story raises this as a possibility, though its content is not yet given.
